configuration.note: Bounds, opacity and the data URI are checked in validateWorkflow; the georeference's CORRECTNESS is not checkable here and is recorded as not established in experiment 143.

ports.note: The `ground` port type was added to the closed union for this widget, which is a base-contract change made deliberately under D4. A plate must not reach clip_raster or sample_raster: its pixels are ink, and sampling them returns the colour of a line. The port type makes that connection impossible rather than reporting it after it is made.

ontology.note: GAP, meaning no alignment to an external cartographic vocabulary -- not meaning the terms are undeclared. fw:MapImageInput and fw:MapImage are declared in ontology/runtime.ttl with their properties. The receipt asserts the digest, the pixel dimensions, the four bounds, the ground resolution in metres and `fw:layerRole "context"`, which is the limit stated where a reader meets the layer rather than only in a document.

changes.description: Draws a scanned or published map under a workflow, in the workflow's own projection, as ground. Built for Snow's 1855 Map 2, whose georeference the South London example has carried since 2026-10-24 with nothing able to read it. See docs/experiments/143-a-georeferenced-plate-as-ground.md.

Refuses a rotated world file by name. Drawing a rotated plate as an upright rectangle would put the map in the wrong place while looking correct, which is a hard stop rather than a limitation. A world file whose origin is the centre of the top-left pixel is read as such, so the extent runs half a pixel further out on each side.
Refuses corners outside CRS84 degrees, which usually means a projected georeference. Reading one datum's coordinates as another's moves a map by hundreds of metres and looks like a correct map.

evidence.note: Nine unit tests over the world-file reader, the extent it derives, the ground resolution and each refusal: a rotated world file, a flipped image, crossed corners, corners outside the world, and a projection that sends the plate nowhere finite. Checked against the example's own geo/map2.jgw byte for byte. That the georeference is CORRECT. The control points were placed by a reader of the plate and this draws what they recorded; an alignment error looks exactly like a correct placement. Measuring the residual against modern boundaries is what would close it. That a reader understands what a historical wash means. The plate's own legend and the example's prose do that work. That 1002x788 over South London, about 40 m per pixel, is enough for anything but ground. There is nothing here for a lab check to recompute -- placing an image where its georeference says has no second implementation that could disagree -- so widgets/check-coverage.json records `none` with that reason rather than claiming parity this project's arithmetic would be agreeing with itself about.
